questions.question: SQL Joins — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, CROSS, and SELF Joins
questions.title: SQL Joins — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, CROSS, and SELF Joins
questions.direct_answer: SQL joins combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column. INNER JOIN returns only matching rows. LEFT JOIN returns all left-side rows with NULLs for non-matches on the right. RIGHT JOIN is the mirror. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps all rows from both sides. CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product. SELF JOIN joins a table to itself for hierarchical or comparison queries.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the NULL-handling behavior of each join type and can choose the correct one for a query requirement, not just recite definitions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using LEFT JOIN but adding a WHERE clause on the right table's column, which silently converts it to an INNER JOIN by filtering out NULL rows.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how the query planner chooses between nested loop, hash join, and merge join algorithms, and why indexing join columns is critical for performance.

sections.title: A Join Is a Row-Matching Rule — The Difference Is What Happens When Rows Don’t Match
sections.content:
Most developers learn joins as "combining two tables." That mental model is incomplete and leads to real bugs because it obscures the most important question: **what happens to rows that find no match on the other side?**

Every join starts the same way — the engine evaluates each row from the left table against rows in the right table using the ON condition. INNER JOIN discards unmatched rows from both sides. LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills the right side with NULLs when no match exists. RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from **both** sides, NULL-padding whichever side is missing. CROSS JOIN skips the ON clause entirely and pairs every row with every other row. SELF JOIN is simply any of these applied to the same table under different aliases.

The reason this matters beyond textbook definitions: the interplay between join type and WHERE versus ON clause placement is the single most common source of join-related bugs in production SQL. Understanding that distinction — what gets filtered during matching versus what gets filtered after — is what separates someone who writes correct queries from someone who copies answers and adjusts until the output looks right.

sections.title: How Each Join Handles Non-Matching Rows
sections.content:
| Join Type | Matching Rows | Left Unmatched | Right Unmatched | Typical Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| INNER | Returned | Discarded | Discarded | Only records existing in both tables |
| LEFT (OUTER) | Returned | Kept, right side = NULL | Discarded | All left rows + optional match |
| RIGHT (OUTER) | Returned | Discarded | Kept, left side = NULL | Mirror of LEFT — rarely needed |
| FULL OUTER | Returned | Kept, right = NULL | Kept, left = NULL | Reconciling two incomplete datasets |
| CROSS | All combinations | N/A (no ON clause) | N/A | Generating permutations, size × color |
| SELF | Same as chosen type | Depends on INNER/LEFT | Depends on INNER/LEFT | Hierarchies, row-to-row comparisons |

sections.title: The Bug Everyone Writes: How WHERE Silently Converts LEFT JOIN to INNER
sections.content:
This is the most common join bug in production SQL, and it’s subtle because the query runs without errors — it just returns wrong results.

Consider two tables: `orders` and `shipments`. You want all orders, including unshipped ones, but only showing FedEx shipments where they exist. The natural first attempt looks right:

```sql
-- BUG: silently drops all unshipped orders
SELECT o.id, o.total, s.shipped_at
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN shipments s ON o.id = s.order_id
WHERE s.carrier = 'FedEx';
```

`WHERE` runs **after** the join produces its result set. For unshipped orders, every column from `shipments` is NULL. The condition `NULL = 'FedEx'` evaluates to UNKNOWN — not FALSE, not TRUE — and `WHERE` discards any row that isn’t TRUE. Your LEFT JOIN just became an INNER JOIN.

The fix is moving the condition into the ON clause, where it participates in the matching logic instead of the filtering logic:

```sql
-- CORRECT: unshipped orders still appear with NULL shipment columns
SELECT o.id, o.total, s.shipped_at
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN shipments s ON o.id = s.order_id
                     AND s.carrier = 'FedEx';
```

Now the ON clause says "match orders to shipments, but only FedEx shipments." Orders with no shipment — or only non-FedEx shipments — still appear with NULLs on the right side. The rule is simple: **conditions on the preserved table go in WHERE, conditions on the optional table go in ON.** Once you internalize this, you’ll catch the bug in code review before it reaches production.

sections.title: SELF JOIN and CROSS JOIN — The Two Variants That Catch People in Interviews
sections.content:
**SELF JOIN** is not a separate syntax — it’s any join where the same table appears twice under different aliases. The classic use case is hierarchical data like an employee-manager relationship.

```sql
-- Find each employee with their manager's name
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
```

The LEFT JOIN is deliberate. The CEO has a NULL `manager_id`, so an INNER JOIN would silently exclude them from the results — a bug that only surfaces when someone notices the top of the org chart is missing. SELF JOINs also solve comparison problems: finding customers who ordered the same product, detecting duplicate entries, or comparing a row against its previous version in an audit table.

**CROSS JOIN** produces the Cartesian product — every row from the left paired with every row from the right. A `sizes` table with 3 rows crossed with a `colors` table with 5 rows produces all 15 size-color combinations for a product catalog.

```sql
SELECT s.name AS size, c.name AS color
FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colors c;
-- 3 × 5 = 15 rows
```

The danger is scale. Two tables of 10,000 rows produce **100 million rows**. An accidental CROSS JOIN — typically caused by forgetting the ON clause in what was meant to be an INNER JOIN — is one of the fastest ways to bring a database to its knees. Legitimate CROSS JOINs should be limited to small reference tables where the output size is predictable and bounded.

sections.title: Why Join Column Indexes Determine Whether Your Query Takes 2ms or 20 Seconds
sections.content:
The query planner chooses between three join algorithms, and which one it picks determines whether your query completes in milliseconds or minutes on large tables.

**Nested Loop Join** iterates through the outer table and, for each row, looks up matching rows in the inner table. Without an index on the join column, this is O(n × m) — catastrophic for large tables. With a B-tree index on the inner table’s join column, each lookup becomes O(log m), making the total O(n log m). PostgreSQL favors nested loops when the inner table is small or has a highly selective index.

**Hash Join** builds an in-memory hash table from the smaller table, then probes it with each row from the larger table. Total cost is O(n + m), but it requires enough `work_mem` to hold the hash table — if it spills to disk, performance degrades significantly. The planner uses hash joins when no useful index exists and one table is substantially smaller.

**Merge Join** sorts both tables on the join column, then merges them in one linear pass. The sorts cost O(n log n + m log m), but if both sides already provide sorted access through an index, the sort cost drops to zero. Merge joins excel at large-to-large table joins where both sides have sorted indexes.

The practical rule: **always index foreign key columns used in joins.** PostgreSQL does not automatically create indexes on foreign keys — unlike MySQL’s InnoDB. A missing index on `shipments.order_id` forces every join to the `orders` table into a sequential scan or hash join. Adding a B-tree index on that single column can reduce a 15-second query to under 5 milliseconds. Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to verify which algorithm the planner chose and whether it’s using your indexes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **WHERE on a right-table column converts LEFT JOIN to INNER** — `WHERE orders.status = 'ACTIVE'` filters out NULLs, silently dropping all unmatched left rows; move the condition to the ON clause to preserve them
- **INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows from both sides** — any row without a counterpart on the other side disappears from the result; use LEFT JOIN when unmatched left rows matter
- **SELF JOIN requires two aliases** — `employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id = e2.id`; the standard query pattern for hierarchical data like org charts and category trees
- **CROSS JOIN is Cartesian — always intentional** — 100 x 200 = 20,000 rows; never write it by accident; used for generating test combinations or date ranges
- **Index the join column on both sides** — the planner selects hash join for large unindexed tables; nested loop + index scan for small or indexed ones; an unindexed FK causes a full scan on every join

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Most people learn joins as "combining two tables" — but the more precise framing is: what happens to a row that finds no match on the other side? That one question explains the difference between every join type.

**INNER JOIN — matched rows only**
- Returns only rows where both sides have a match — so `orders INNER JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id` excludes any order whose `customer_id` doesn't exist in customers, which means orphaned rows are silently dropped from the result
- This is the most common join and the default when you write just `JOIN` without a qualifier

**LEFT JOIN — all from the left, matched or not**
- Returns every row from the left table, with NULL values on the right side for rows that find no match — so `customers LEFT JOIN orders` returns customers who have never placed an order, with null in every order column
- The critical trap: adding `WHERE orders.status = 'ACTIVE'` after a LEFT JOIN silently converts it to an INNER JOIN, because null values fail the WHERE filter — move status filtering into the ON clause to preserve unmatched left rows

**CROSS JOIN and SELF JOIN**
- CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product — every left row paired with every right row; 100 rows x 200 rows = 20,000 result rows; useful for generating combinations or test data, almost never accidental
- SELF JOIN joins a table to itself using two aliases, which is the standard way to query hierarchies — `employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id = e2.id` fetches each employee alongside their manager's name

Always index the join column on both sides — the planner chooses between nested loop, hash join, and merge join based on table sizes and index availability; an unindexed foreign key forces a sequential scan on the larger table for every join.

questions.question: SQL Subqueries vs Joins — Performance and When to Use Each
questions.title: SQL Subqueries vs Joins — Performance and When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: Joins and subqueries can often express the same logic, but they differ in readability, performance, and capability. Joins combine rows from multiple tables in the FROM clause. Subqueries are nested queries that can appear in SELECT, FROM, WHERE, or HAVING. Modern planners often optimize uncorrelated subqueries to the same plan as a join, but correlated subqueries execute once per outer row and can be dramatically slower.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when the planner can optimize a subquery to a join and when it cannot, particularly the performance trap of correlated subqueries.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing correlated subqueries without realizing they execute once per outer row, turning an O(n) join into an O(n²) operation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that EXISTS subqueries often outperform IN subqueries on large datasets because EXISTS short-circuits on the first match, while IN must build the entire result set.

sections.title: The Planner Rewrites Most Subqueries Into Joins — The Ones It Can't Are the Ones That Hurt
sections.content:
The debate between joins and subqueries is mostly a readability choice — **until a correlated subquery sneaks in.** Modern query planners (PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8.0+) routinely flatten uncorrelated subqueries into semi-joins or hash joins, producing the exact same execution plan you'd get from writing the join yourself. The SQL you write and the SQL the engine runs are often different.

The dangerous case is the **correlated subquery**: an inner query that references a column from the outer query. Because the inner query's result depends on the current outer row, the planner cannot flatten it — it must execute the inner query once per outer row. A 100,000-row table means 100,000 executions of the inner query. What looked like a clean one-liner is hiding an O(n²) operation.

Understanding which subqueries the planner can rewrite and which it can't is the difference between writing readable SQL and writing accidentally slow SQL.

sections.title: When the Planner Can Optimize and When It Can't
sections.content:
| Pattern | Planner Behavior | Performance |
|---|---|---|
| `WHERE id IN (SELECT ...)` uncorrelated | Rewritten to semi-join | Same as explicit JOIN |
| `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT ...)` uncorrelated | Rewritten to semi-join | Same as JOIN, short-circuits |
| `FROM (SELECT ... GROUP BY) AS sub` | Executes subquery once, joins result | Fine — useful for pre-aggregation |
| `SELECT (SELECT ... WHERE inner.x = outer.x)` correlated | Executes per outer row | O(n²) risk — rewrite as JOIN |
| `WHERE col IN (SELECT ... WHERE inner.x = outer.x)` correlated | Executes per outer row | O(n²) risk — rewrite as JOIN |
| `JOIN ... ON` | Direct execution plan | Baseline — what subqueries get rewritten to |

sections.title: The Correlated Subquery Trap — When Your O(n) Query Secretly Runs O(n²)
sections.content:
A correlated subquery references the outer query, so the engine must re-evaluate the inner query for every outer row. The result looks correct but the execution time grows quadratically with table size.

```sql
-- CORRELATED: runs the customer lookup once per order row
SELECT o.id, o.total,
    (SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE c.id = o.customer_id) AS customer_name
FROM orders o;

-- EQUIVALENT JOIN: single pass, same result
SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name AS customer_name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

On a table with 100K orders, the correlated version runs the customer lookup 100,000 times. The join does it in a single hash join pass. In practice this means the join completes in ~50ms while the correlated subquery takes 5–10 seconds. The rule: **if a subquery in SELECT or WHERE references the outer table, rewrite it as a JOIN.** Always verify with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` — the plan will show "SubPlan" for correlated execution versus "Hash Semi Join" for the optimized path.

sections.title: EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN — When Subqueries Actually Win
sections.content:
Not all subqueries are inferior to joins. **`EXISTS` subqueries can outperform both `IN` and `JOIN`** when checking for the presence of related rows in a large table, because EXISTS **short-circuits on the first match**.

```sql
-- EXISTS: stops scanning as soon as it finds one match per customer
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);

-- IN: builds the entire set of customer_ids from orders first
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);

-- JOIN: may produce duplicates if a customer has multiple orders
SELECT DISTINCT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
```

With 10,000 customers and 5 million orders, `EXISTS` checks each customer and stops at the first matching order — at most 10,000 index probes. `IN` must first build a set of all distinct customer_ids from 5M rows. The `JOIN` approach is also fast but requires `DISTINCT` to de-duplicate customers with multiple orders, adding a sort or hash step.

The practical guide: use **JOIN** when you need columns from both tables. Use **EXISTS** for "has at least one" checks on large tables. Use **IN** for small, static value lists. Avoid correlated subqueries in SELECT clauses — rewrite as joins.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Correlated subquery runs once per outer row** — it references the outer query, so it re-executes for each row; at N rows the subquery runs N times, creating O(n squared) complexity vs a join's O(n)
- **Uncorrelated subqueries are often rewritten to joins** — PostgreSQL 16 and MySQL 8.0+ flatten `IN (SELECT ...)` into hash joins at the planning stage; verify with `EXPLAIN` before manually rewriting
- **`EXISTS` short-circuits; `IN` materializes** — `EXISTS` stops on the first match; `IN (SELECT ...)` collects the entire result set before comparing; `EXISTS` wins for large existence checks
- **`NOT IN` breaks on NULL** — if any value in the subquery is NULL, `NOT IN` returns no rows due to three-valued logic; always use `NOT EXISTS` for nullable FK columns
- **CTEs (WITH) are not always optimization fences** — PostgreSQL 12+ inlines non-recursive CTEs by default; wrapping a subquery in a CTE no longer forces materialization

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Joins and subqueries can often express the same query — and modern query planners frequently rewrite one into the other. The performance difference only becomes critical in one specific scenario: the correlated subquery.

**When they're equivalent — let the planner decide**
- An uncorrelated subquery doesn't reference the outer query's row — PostgreSQL and MySQL 8.0+ routinely rewrite these into equivalent joins at the planning stage, so the execution plan is the same regardless of which form you write
- In these cases, write whichever reads more clearly; the performance difference is negligible because the planner will optimize it either way

**The correlated subquery trap**
- A correlated subquery references the outer query's current row — `SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.total > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = o.customer_id)` — which means the subquery runs once for every row in the outer scan, turning an O(n) operation into O(n squared)
- At 100,000 orders across 10,000 customers, that's 100,000 subquery executions — where a single join with a GROUP BY pre-computes the average once per customer

**EXISTS vs IN — for existence checks**
- `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)` short-circuits on the first match — as soon as one order is found, the check succeeds — which makes it faster than `IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`, which must collect and materialize the full set before comparing
- Use `NOT EXISTS` instead of `NOT IN` when nullable columns are involved — `NOT IN` returns no rows if any value in the subquery is NULL due to three-valued logic; `NOT EXISTS` handles nulls correctly

Use a join when you need columns from both tables. Use a subquery when the logic reads more naturally as a nested question. Use `EXISTS` for existence checks on large tables.
